header.title: Aymeri de Narbonne (D): AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Anonymous
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's urn:geste:ed-aimerid:dipl, from the Geste corpus of chansons de geste, Camps et al. (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.

notes.1041: Line 1049: vont la briche querant, literally 'go seeking the briche' (a trap, or a losing game); taken as 'are wasting their effort'.
notes.3505: Lines 3510-3513 are taken as one sentence: no one could imagine a bird whose figure was not on the tree. Line 3516: the river of Paradise, from which precious stones were said to come. Line 3524: por coi taken as 'provided that'. Line 3528: Escler, 'Slavs', a stock name for pagan peoples.

nodes.text: They have set so many carpenters to the work
that by morning they had the engines standing upright.
They go hauling the siege tower toward the city;
archers and men-at-arms climbed up on top.
When the Saracens and Persians have seen it,
one said to the other: “The French are very cunning;
now they are bringing a great enchantment against us.
We are all dead, beaten and forced to yield.
Our messengers are on a fool's errand;
before we have help from the emir
as marvellous as you will hear me tell.
In the middle of the hall of the princely palace
there was a tree that had been made there;
it was made of copper, and they had had it gilded,
and melted and cast in a mould.
There is no man under heaven, however well he could imagine
and observe the ways of birds,
who could not find on that tree
the true likeness of every bird.
And each bird had its mate.
The enchanter deserved high praise:
from the river that you hear called Paradise
he had the stones brought and gathered;
he had had them set in fine enamel.
By necromancy he makes the wind go in
and rise upward through the pipe;
when the wind blows, it makes the birds sing,
each in their own way, softly and clearly.
There is no man under heaven who could have his fill of it.
If he is angry, as long as he hears it sound,
at once it makes him forget his anger.
As long as one wishes, one makes the sound last,
and when one wishes, one makes it stop.
Saracens and Slavs serve the emir;
he has himself greatly served and honoured.
The lady hears him and has bowed toward him.
All night long they made great joy.
Count Aymeri, of the bold face,
sent for a physician without further delay;
he had once been a pagan, from beyond the salt sea.
He very quickly mixed a potion;
he has bandaged Aymeri's wound
and made the potion go down into his body.
Before morning came, at daybreak,
he was sounder than a peeled apple.
In the early morning, when dawn had broken,
they have richly adorned Hermengart.
